complete_examples.overview: Three worked reviews. Each shows the scope, the reasoning, and the shape of the report. The report text is the style target: plain English, short sentences, verdict first.

example.name: diff_review_with_a_crash
example.scenario: The user says: "review this change before I merge". The diff adds a method that writes a row to the Gantt table.

step.approach: Read the agent contract and the table schema note. Confirm that Start is required and Finish is optional for milestones.
step.expected_outcome: The rule is clear: Finish may be null. The code calls Value on it. That is a crash.

step.approach: Follow the caller. Confirm nothing upstream guarantees Finish.
step.analysis: A milestone row reaches this method with Finish null. The Value call throws. The user sees a generic error and the chart stops.
Only the happy path is tested. No test feeds a null Finish or a blank Name.

step.approach: One P0, one P1, one P2. Detail all three. Show the fix once.

key_takeaways.takeaway: Read the contract before the code. It turns a hunch into a blocker.
One code sample can fix two findings. Do not paste the same block twice.
An open question goes in its own section, not inside a finding.

example.name: plan_review_for_risk
example.scenario: The user says: "review this plan before I start". The plan describes replacing the refresh path.

step.approach: List every claim the plan makes about behaviour, performance, and scope.
step.expected_outcome: Seven claims. Two are unproven. One contradicts the current contract.

step.description: Check each claim against the code and the contract
step.approach: Read the current refresh path and the contract statement about refresh triggering.
step.analysis: The plan says selection changes will trigger a refresh. The contract forbids that. This is a blocker, and it is cheap to fix now.

step.description: Rank by cost to discover late
step.approach: Order the risks by how expensive they become after the work starts.

example.report:
VERDICT: Do not start until item 1 is resolved. SCOPE: the refresh replacement plan, all seven claims. COUNTS: 1 blocker, 1 high, 2 medium.
TOP RISK: The plan makes selection changes render. The contract forbids it.
FINDINGS
### 1. Selection changes would render (P0, contract) Where: plan section 3, step 2 What happens: the plan wires selection events into the refresh. Why it matters: this breaks a stated invariant. It also makes the chart redraw while the user is reading it. Fix: route only chart-affecting edits and chart-setting commands to the refresh. Leave selection alone. Cost if found late: the whole event layer is rewritten.
### 2. "Much faster" is not measured (P1) Where: plan section 1 What happens: the goal states a speed-up with no number and no baseline. Why it matters: you cannot tell success from failure at the end. Fix: state the current duration and the target. Name the test that measures it.
### 3. Rollback is not described (P2) Where: plan section 5 What happens: no way back if the new path misbehaves. Why it matters: this path renders every book. A bad build reaches every user. Fix: keep the old path behind one switch for one release.
### 4. The plan has no slice boundary (P2) Where: plan section 2 What happens: one large change with no intermediate green states. Why it matters: no safe point to stop, review, or revert. Fix: split into three slices, each shippable on its own.
NEXT: architect mode revises items 1 and 2. Then this mode re-reviews the plan.

key_takeaways.takeaway: Review the plan's claims, not its prose.
Rank by the cost of finding the problem late.
A contract break in a plan is cheaper to fix than in code. Say so.

example.name: area_health_audit
example.scenario: The user says: "this folder is getting hard to work in, audit it". The folder has nine files and about 2,400 lines.

step.approach: List the files. Read the public surface of each one. Note who calls whom.
step.analysis: Three files hold most of the logic. Two are near-duplicates. One utility class is used by everything.

step.approach: For each of the three largest files, count the reasons to change and the callers.
step.analysis: The renderer has six reasons to change. Every change touches the utility class.

step.approach: Pick the two or three changes with the highest return. Do not produce a rewrite plan.

example.report:
VERDICT: Healthy enough to change. Two fixes will pay for themselves. SCOPE: nine files, about 2,400 lines. Tests were read, not run. COUNTS: 0 blockers, 2 high, 3 medium.
TOP RISK: Every change touches one shared helper, so every change carries the same regression risk.
FINDINGS
### 1. The renderer has six reasons to change (P1) Where: ChartRenderer.cs, 940 lines What happens: parsing, geometry, styling, drawing, logging, and cleanup live together. Why it matters: a style change can break geometry, and no test separates them. Fix: split along the existing seams. Start with geometry, because it has the most tests.
### 2. Two files are near-duplicates (P1) Where: ShapePainter.cs and RasterPainter.cs What happens: about 70 percent of the drawing code is copied. Why it matters: every fix must be made twice. One copy already differs by accident. Fix: extract the shared pass. Keep two thin adapters for the platform calls.
### 3. One helper is a global dependency (P2) Where: SheetUtil.cs What happens: twelve files call it for unrelated reasons. Why it matters: any change to it is a change to the whole area. Fix: split it by purpose. Move each group next to its only caller.
### 4. Risk-weighted coverage is uneven (P2) Where: tests What happens: parsing is well tested. Cleanup and failure paths are not. Why it matters: the untested paths are the ones that corrupt state. Fix: add tests for the two cleanup paths before the next refactor.
### 5. Logging is mixed with logic (P3) Where: across the folder What happens: log calls sit inside calculations. Why it matters: tests capture noise, and the log level changes the flow. Fix: return a result and log at the boundary. Low urgency.
NEXT: code mode takes items 1 and 2 as one slice each. This mode re-reviews after each slice.

key_takeaways.takeaway: An audit ends with a shortlist, not a plan to rewrite everything.
Rank by the cost of change, not by how ugly the code looks.
Name what is healthy. It tells the reader what not to touch.
